title: Building a retrieval cascade
summary: A cascade is a funnel where each stage costs more per item and sees fewer items. What breaks is never the stages, it is the contract between them: fetching the text, removing duplicates, and what happens when a stage fails. Measured here, 38 percent of a top 20 candidate list was repeat documents.
html:
You have two stages now. A cheap one that can look at everything, and an expensive one that can look at a few things properly. Today is wiring them into one path, and the things that go wrong when you do.

Almost none of the trouble is in the stages. It is all in the contract between them.

The shape

1,000,000 documents
     |   vector or BM25 search
    100 candidates
     |   cross-encoder reranking
      5 chunks
     |   the language model
      1 answer

The design principle is that each stage costs roughly a thousand times more per item than the one before it, and sees roughly a thousandth as many items. Multiply those together and every stage costs about the same. That is what a balanced cascade looks like.

The analogy is airport security. Everyone walks through the metal detector, which is fast, cheap and sets off false alarms constantly. The people who beep get the hand wand, which is slower and more accurate. A handful get the full search. Nobody would full-search every passenger, and nobody would wave the whole queue through on the metal detector alone.

Where your latency actually goes

Rough but useful numbers for the sketch above. Vector search over a million vectors with a graph index is about 10 milliseconds. A cross-encoder over 100 candidates is about 100. The language model generating an answer from 5 chunks is about a second.

So retrieval is something like a tenth of the user's wait and generation is the rest. Worth sitting with, because it means the retrieval budget is far more generous than people act like it is. Teams agonise over shaving 20 milliseconds off a vector search while a second of generation sits next to it unexamined. If you can spend 50 extra milliseconds on reranking and get better answers, that trade is almost always worth taking.

Four things in the contract

One: somebody has to fetch the text. Your vector index returns IDs and scores. Your reranker needs the actual words. If the text is not in the index, you now do a hundred random reads against a document store. A hundred serial reads at 20 milliseconds each is two seconds, which is twenty times your whole reranking budget, and it never appears in anyone's architecture diagram. Batch the fetch, or keep the text next to the vectors, but do not discover this in production.

Two: deduplicate before you rerank. Two sources of duplicates. Overlapping chunks from day 6 mean the same paragraph appears in two chunks by construction. And if your first stage is a hybrid from day 34, the word index and the vector index return overlapping sets. Every duplicate in your candidate list is a slot of reranker budget spent on something you already have, and a top 5 that turns out to be one document five times.

Three: do not let stage one's score into the final ordering. Once the reranker has spoken, rank by its score alone. Blending a BM25 score with a reranker score is day 34's incomparable numbers problem, reintroduced on purpose. If you want to blend, use ranks, not scores.

Four: decide now what happens when the reranker is down. It is a model call on the critical path. When it times out, serve stage one's ordering and log it. A slightly worse answer beats an error page, and that choice is much easier to make calmly today than at 2am.

If you want to see it measured

I chunked the 38 published lessons into 200 token windows with 40 of overlap, which gave 263 chunks, then ran four queries and looked at what a top 20 candidate list is actually made of.

query                                     distinct lessons   worst single lesson
"how much overlap between chunks"             14 of 20            3 slots
"why does brute force search get slow"         9 of 20            4 slots
"how do I make my vectors take less memory"   17 of 20            3 slots
"how are the weights in BM25 computed"        10 of 20            5 slots

average: 12.5 distinct lessons per top 20

So about 38 percent of the candidate slots were repeat documents, and on one query a single lesson took five of the twenty. If you rerank that list and keep the top 5 without deduplicating, you are quite likely to hand the model the same lesson three times and call it three pieces of evidence.

Second measurement, on how much two first stage systems overlap. Same two lexical systems as day 34, a full text index and a title index, taking the top k from each:

top 3 each    2 shared, 4 in the union
top 10 each   4 shared, 16 in the union
top 20 each  11 shared, 29 in the union

The interesting row is the first one. At the very top, where it matters, the two systems barely agree: two of their three best guesses are shared, which is another way of seeing why fusion is worth doing. The bottom row I do not trust at all, because 20 out of 38 documents is more than half my corpus, so of course the sets collide. That is a measurement artifact of a tiny corpus and I would be misleading you if I quoted it as a general number.

One opinion

More than two retrieval stages almost never pays. Three stage retrieval plus generation is usually a sign that nobody measured where the quality was actually being lost. That is my read rather than a result I can point at, but the cheap way to check it is day 38's recall curve: if stage one's ceiling is already high, a third stage has nothing to find.

If you remember one thing
The stages are easy. The contract between them is where the bugs live: who fetches the text, who removes duplicates, whose score decides the order, and what happens when a stage fails.

Tomorrow: using a language model itself as the reranker, which is tempting, expensive, and has a failure mode the cross-encoder does not.
exercise:
One. Write your day 39 note.

Two. Take the four contract items and answer them for a retrieval system you work with, or one you can read the code of. Who fetches the document text, and is that fetch batched? Is there any deduplication before the final selection? Does the first stage score influence the final order? What happens today if the last stage throws? Most systems fail two of the four, and finding out which two takes about ten minutes.
